title: How to know when you are overengineering: if you cannot name the incident that justified it, you are building for an imaginary future
story:
Overengineering is hard to catch in yourself because it is indistinguishable, at the moment of doing it, from competence. Both look like thinking ahead. Both involve considering what might go wrong. The engineer adding a layer of indirection for a future requirement and the engineer adding one for a requirement that will never exist are doing the same thing and feeling the same way about it.

So the question of whether you are doing it cannot be answered by introspection, and the reliable test is external: name the specific event this complexity is a response to.

A real constraint can be named. The incident where the deployment failed because two services had incompatible assumptions. The customer who needed their data in a separate region. The outage that happened because a single database could not absorb the write volume. These are events with dates. An imagined constraint can only be described, and the description is always in the future tense and the conditional mood — in case we need to, when we scale to, if we ever want to. That difference in grammar is a more reliable signal than any amount of architectural judgement, because it is about evidence rather than about plausibility, and the imagined constraints are entirely plausible. That is why they are convincing.

The argument that this is not merely a matter of taste comes from John Gall, in Systemantics: How Systems Work and Especially How They Fail, published in 1975, which states what is now known as Gall's law: a complex system that works is invariably found to have evolved from a simple system that worked; a complex system designed from scratch never works and cannot be patched up to make it work, so one has to start over with a working simple system.

That is a much stronger claim than the usual advice to keep things simple, and it is worth taking at full strength. It is not saying complex systems are harder to build or riskier. It is saying the working ones got there by a particular route, and that the other route does not arrive — that a complex system designed from scratch cannot be repaired into working, so the effort spent is not partially recovered but lost, and the remedy is to start again from something simple that works.

Whether the claim is literally true in every case is arguable. What is not arguable is the mechanism it points at. A simple system that works provides something to test the next increment against, and each addition is validated by a system that was already functioning. A complex system designed up front has no such reference point: when it does not work, the question of which part is wrong has no small answer, because nothing in it has ever worked in isolation.

The cost of the test should be stated honestly, because it is real. Requiring a named incident is conservative by construction, and it will refuse some complexity that turns out to be needed — you will occasionally build the simple thing, hit the wall, and do the work later under time pressure, which is more expensive than having done it up front. That is the trade being made deliberately: paying more for the complexity you actually need, in exchange for not paying at all for the complexity you do not.

What makes the trade favourable is not the price of each decision but the ratio of how often each case occurs. Anticipated requirements that arrive are rarer than anticipated requirements that do not, and the cost of unnecessary complexity is not paid once at build time — it is paid on every subsequent change, by everyone who has to understand the structure before they can alter anything inside it.

There is one genuine exception worth naming, since the rule is otherwise easy to over-apply. Some decisions are expensive to reverse in proportion to how long they have been in place, and for those the calculation changes. Anything that determines a data model, a persistence format or a public interface deserves more anticipation than the test alone would license, because the cost of being wrong grows rather than staying constant. Almost nothing else does.

problem.name: The named incident test
problem.shape: A design includes structure whose purpose is to accommodate something that has not happened.
tell: the justification uses the future tense and the conditional mood
an abstraction has exactly one implementation
the scale being designed for exceeds the current scale by orders of magnitude
nobody can point to an event that prompted the design
problem.move: Require a specific event with a date as the justification for each piece of complexity. Where the justification can only be described rather than named, build the simple version — except where the decision is expensive to reverse in proportion to its age, which is a small and identifiable category.
problem.invariant: A real constraint can be named as an event; an imagined one can only be described. The grammar of the justification distinguishes them more reliably than judgements about plausibility, because the imagined ones are entirely plausible.
problem.breaks: The test is conservative by construction and will occasionally refuse complexity that was needed, which is then built later under pressure at greater cost. And it under-serves decisions whose reversal cost grows with time — data models, persistence formats, public interfaces — where more anticipation is warranted than a named incident would license.

cost.time: work done later, under time pressure, for the cases where the anticipated need was real
cost.beats: designing for the anticipated case, which is cheaper if the case arrives and is paid on every change if it does not, and adding nothing ever, which is cheapest until a reversal cost has been allowed to grow

problem.practice: Take the most elaborate piece of structure in your current system and ask what event caused it. If the answer is in the future tense, you have found the thing to simplify — and if it is a data model or a public interface, you have found the exception instead.

beats.broke: Complexity is added for a future that is described rather than observed, and at the moment of adding it, it is indistinguishable from competence — both look like thinking ahead.
beats.fix: Require a specific event as the justification for each piece of complexity, since a real constraint can be named with a date and an imagined one can only be described in the conditional.
beats.cost: The test is conservative by construction and will refuse some complexity that was needed, which then gets built later under pressure — the deliberate trade being to pay more for what you need and nothing for what you do not.

interview.q: How do you tell a design that anticipates a real requirement from one that speculates about an imaginary one?
interview.trap: Judging by whether the anticipated requirement is plausible. Imagined constraints are entirely plausible — that is what makes them persuasive — so filtering on plausibility filters nothing.
interview.answer:
By asking what event the design is a response to, and listening to the grammar of the answer.
